blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: State the forms of money, name its functions and its characteristics, and keep the two lists apart.

blocks.heading: What money is
blocks.text: Money is anything that people generally accept as payment for goods and services and for settling debts. What makes a thing money is the acceptance it carries, not its material, and money today appears as coins, notes and bank deposits moved by card or phone. A trader at the Katutura open market takes a N$20 note for tomatoes as readily as a card payment: both are money, because both are accepted. In Germany the euro plays the same role in a Munich bakery that the Namibian dollar plays in Windhoek.

blocks.heading: What money does
blocks.text: The functions of money are the jobs it does in exchange. As a medium of exchange it passes from buyer to seller: a wood-carver in Katutura sells a carving for N$80 and buys a bag of maize meal for N$45 the same afternoon, where barter would need one trader who both wants a carving and sells maize - a double coincidence of wants. As a unit of account it measures value, so Etosha Gate Lodge can quote a night at N$1 200 and compare it with the cost of providing it. As a store of value it keeps worth from one week to the next, so a worker paid on Friday can spend part of it on Sunday.

blocks.heading: Store of value, and its limit
blocks.text: Of the three functions, store of value carries a condition. Money can be kept and spent later without rotting, unlike the fish or tomatoes it might buy, so a fisher in Lüderitz who earns most of her income in the lobster season can keep notes and bank deposits and spend them through the quiet months. But money keeps its buying power best while prices are fairly steady. If prices rise by 10% in a year, N$1 000 saved at the start buys about what N$909 would have bought before, so savers lose. When prices rise very fast, people tend to swap money for goods, cattle or foreign currency that hold their value better, and money does this job badly. The other two functions can carry on even then: money still changes hands and still measures prices.

blocks.heading: What money needs to be
blocks.text: The characteristics of money are the qualities a thing needs before people accept it as money. Acceptability: sellers take it in payment. Durability: it survives being passed around. Portability: a N$100 note carries its buying power in a pocket, which a goat cannot. Divisibility: it splits into small units for small purchases. Uniformity: one N$50 note matches another, so a buyer need not inspect it. Scarcity: it is limited in supply, so it tends to hold its value.

blocks.heading: Two lists, not one
blocks.text: Learners often mix up the characteristics of money and the functions of money, but they are different lists. The functions are what money does in an exchange: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value. The characteristics are what money has to be to do those jobs: acceptable, durable, portable, divisible, uniform, scarce. The test is to ask 'is it' or 'does it': 'it passes from buyer to seller' names a function, while 'it survives being passed around' names a characteristic. A learner who answers a characteristics question with 'medium of exchange' has quoted the wrong list.
